summary: A landlocked country in the West African Sahel, formerly called Upper Volta and renamed Burkina Faso in 1984 (meaning 'land of upright people'), known for the tradition of the Mossi kingdoms and for the Pan-African film festival (FESPACO).

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived in the 14th and 15th centuries with Mandinka (Dyula) merchants and the trade network of the Mali Empire, but the rulers of the Mossi kingdoms long maintained traditional religion, and Islam spread mainly among merchants and the Fulani. The jihad movements of the 19th century and the expansion of trade in the colonial period let Islam spread rapidly in the countryside, and today about two thirds of the population are Muslims, mainly Sunni.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced in 1900 by missionaries of the White Fathers, who founded the first mission station at Koupéla in 1901. During the French colonial period Catholic schools trained many officials and intellectuals, so Catholics are over-represented among the national elite. Catholic influence is especially strong in the capital, Ouagadougou, which Pope John Paul II visited in 1990.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Traditional belief centers on ancestor worship, earth deities and mask rituals, such as the earth priests of the Mossi and the mask societies of the Bobo. With the expansion of Islam and Christianity, the population following purely traditional belief has gradually declined, but many Muslims and Christians still take part in traditional rituals and initiation rites.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced in the 1920s by missionaries of the American Assemblies of God (Pentecostal), who set up churches and schools in the Mossi region. After independence Protestant churches continued to grow, with Pentecostals and Evangelicals in particular attracting many believers in cities and among young people.

religion.background: From the 15th century the Mossi kingdoms arose in what is now central Burkina Faso, where the king (the Mogho Naba) also held a religious status and traditional belief was at the center of the state. Islam came with the trans-Saharan trade and Dyula merchants and expanded greatly in the 19th century and the colonial period. After France conquered the Mossi kingdoms in 1896, Catholic missionaries arrived in the 1900s and expanded their influence through schooling. Today Burkina Faso is known for peaceful religious coexistence, and a single family often has members of different faiths, but since 2015 attacks by jihadist groups in the north have caused a serious humanitarian crisis.

language.official: After the 2023 constitutional revision, indigenous languages became official languages and French became a working language.

ranking.name: Mooré
ranking.description: Mooré is the language of the largest people, the Mossi, and belongs to the Gur branch. The Mossi kingdoms built a powerful state in the center from the 15th century, with their capital in what is now Ouagadougou, making Mooré the main language and lingua franca of the center. About half of the population speak it as a mother tongue, and after the 2023 constitutional revision it was made an official language together with other indigenous languages.

ranking.name: Fula
ranking.description: Fula is the language of the Fulani (Peul), a nomadic people spread across West Africa, found mainly in the northern Sahel region. In the 19th century the Fulani established polities in the north, and Fula also became the lingua franca of pastoral areas. In recent conflicts in the north the Fulani have often been unfairly linked with armed groups, causing ethnic tension.

ranking.name: Dyula
ranking.description: Dyula is a Mandinka language, mutually intelligible with Bambara in Mali and Dyula in Côte d'Ivoire. It was originally the commercial language of the Dyula merchants, and with interregional trade it came to be widely used in the western city of Bobo-Dioulasso and its surroundings, becoming the market lingua franca of the west; it has few native speakers but many second-language speakers.

language.history: There are about sixty indigenous languages in Burkina Faso, the main ones being Mooré in the center, Fula in the north and Dyula in the west. After French colonization in 1896, French became the language of administration and education, and Upper Volta, independent in 1960, continued with French as the official language. In 1984 the country was renamed Burkina Faso, the name being made up of the Mooré 'Burkina' (upright people) and the Dyula 'Faso' (fatherland), symbolizing the status of indigenous languages. In 2023 the military government revised the constitution to make indigenous languages official languages and French a working language, in order to shake off the influence of the former colonial power.

ranking.name: Tô
ranking.description: A thick, pasty staple made by stirring sorghum, millet or cornmeal into water and cooking it; a piece is pinched off by hand and dipped into okra sauce or leaf-vegetable sauce.
ranking.history: Tô is Burkina Faso's most basic staple; sorghum and millet are the most drought-tolerant crops of the Sahel, and West Africans have grown these grains for thousands of years. In this agricultural landlocked country, most households eat tô almost every day. Maize became widespread only after the colonial period, so the versions made from sorghum and millet are traditionally valued more.

ranking.name: Riz Gras
ranking.description: Rice cooked together with tomato sauce, onion and meat or fish into glossy red rice with a rich aroma, often eaten with vegetables and chili sauce.
ranking.history: Riz gras belongs to the same family as Senegal's 'thieboudienne' and West African jollof rice, and is generally thought to originate with the Wolof of the Senegambia region and then to have spread across West Africa. Rice became widespread during the colonial period and, after independence, with urbanization; 'riz gras' means 'fat rice' in French. In Burkina Faso it is a classic dish for celebrations such as weddings, baptisms and festivals.

ranking.name: Bissap (Hibiscus Drink)
ranking.description: Dried hibiscus calyces are steeped in water to draw out a deep red liquid, flavored with sugar, mint or ginger and drunk cold; it is sweet, sour and refreshing and is the most common street drink.
ranking.history: Hibiscus is native to Africa and is generally thought to have been grown in West Africa and Sudan for thousands of years. In the hot Sahel, the chilled hibiscus drink is the most popular drink for beating the heat, and street vendors often sell it in plastic bags. In Islamic societies where alcohol is forbidden, hibiscus and ginger drinks are also common at gatherings and at the breaking of the fast in Ramadan. 'Zoom-koom' is the Mooré name for a grain drink, often served together with hibiscus drink.

ranking.name: Okra Sauce
ranking.description: A sticky sauce stewed mainly from okra with dried fish, meat, tomato, onion and spices, used to accompany tô or rice.
ranking.history: Okra is native to Africa, generally thought to have been domesticated in Ethiopia or West Africa, and is one of the most important vegetables in West African cooking. During the slave trade okra was carried to the Americas, and the name of the gumbo of the American South comes from the word for okra in West African languages. In Burkina Faso okra sauce is the sauce that every household serves daily with tô, and dried okra powder can also be used in the dry season.

ranking.name: Dolo
ranking.description: A traditional beer brewed by fermenting the liquid from boiled sprouted sorghum; it is low in alcohol, with a sour taste and a grain aroma, and is usually served in calabash gourds and shared among everyone.
ranking.history: Dolo is the traditional sorghum beer of Burkina Faso and neighboring areas, made and sold by women at home or in village brewing houses, and it is an important source of income for many women. It has religious significance in traditional society and is often used in rituals such as the honoring of ancestral spirits, funerals and weddings. With the expansion of Islam, Muslims generally do not drink dolo, but it remains quite important in the social life of Christians and followers of traditional beliefs.
